title: The Satyanarayana katha
hookLine: a merchant keeps putting off a promise to God
carry: a vow to God is kept, not put off
tomorrow: what if the whole universe were one egg?

lines: A STORY READ ON THE FLOOR.
cards: A low table in a living room. A framed picture of Vishnu, bananas, a plate of sweets, and someone reading a story aloud while the family sits on the floor. It might be for a housewarming, a new job, a promise kept.
This is the Satyanarayana katha, and tradition places it in the Skanda Purana. At its center is a merchant who keeps putting off one promise.

teach.b: The question underneath: what happens to a promise you keep putting off?
The katha opens with the sage Narada asking Vishnu how people in hard times can be free of suffering, and Vishnu answers with this worship and its stories. Then the merchant.
He promises to hold the worship if he's blessed with a child. A daughter is born, and he puts it off. He promises again for her wedding, and puts it off again.

His troubles start there, and keep coming until the vow is kept. Later his daughter rushes out without taking the prasad, the blessed food, and loses sight of her husband until she goes back and receives it.

Keep the promise; don't walk past the blessing. That's why so many families call it a vrata, a vow: the worship is a promise to God, and the story is about keeping it. A neighbor tradition says it too.

teach.h: ECCLESIASTES: DEFER NOT TO PAY IT.
teach.b: In Ecclesiastes, in Jewish and Christian scripture: "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it."

teach.h: A RITE, OR NO RITE AT ALL.
teach.b: And the next verse: "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay."
What they share: a promise made to God is meant to be kept, and putting it off is its own kind of breaking.

An honest difference: the katha is itself the worship being promised, and it ends with prasad shared around the room. Ecclesiastes names no rite at all, and says plainly that not vowing is better than a vow left unpaid.

how: Hindu families hold the Satyanarayana puja at home for a housewarming, a new job or a vow fulfilled: the katha is read aloud and prasad is shared. In Jewish and Christian life, Ecclesiastes 5 is read as scripture on keeping vows.

o: a merchant's ledger of debts owed to the gods
the Purana named for Kartikeya, home of many stories
a festival calendar for the month of Kartik

games.q: the katha, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: asks how to be free of suffering

s: in the katha, the merchant keeps his vow right away
he puts it off twice, and his troubles start there.
Ecclesiastes says not vowing is better than a vow left unpaid
'better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.'
the katha and Ecclesiastes teach exactly the same thing
both say keep a vow without delay; the katha is a rite with prasad, and Ecclesiastes names no rite.

games.q: your aunt promised a Satyanarayana puja if her surgery went well. it did, and months later she's still 'meaning to get to it.' by the katha, what's the point?
o: once the good thing has happened, the promise matters less.
the merchant's troubles began when he put it off; keep it, and don't wait.
she should promise an even bigger puja to make up for the delay.
games.why: the katha's merchant promises, is blessed, and delays twice; the story turns on keeping the vow, and not walking past the blessing.

practice: If there's prasad or any small sweet in the house, take a piece in your right hand, or cupped in both, the way families receive prasad at the end of the katha, and eat it slowly.
Then bring to mind one promise you've put off, to God or to someone else, and name the smallest step that would keep it. Hold that step in mind, breathing slowly, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Skanda. The Purana that carries Kartikeya's name, where tradition places the Satyanarayana katha, a story of a promise put off.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Satyanarayana, Vishnu as Narayana, honored with satya, truth, in the name.

carryVoice: Your line: a vow to God is kept, not put off. And don't walk past the blessing. See you tomorrow.
